blocks.text: Draft for Jared's approval. Built from the provincial pages named under Sources, read November 1, 2026.

If you are buying a 55+ home in BC, these provincial rules apply in every strata, whichever city the building is in. They decide who can live in a unit, who can own it, who is exempt from the age limit and whether the unit can be rented. A manufactured-home park is different: it is governed by park tenancy law, not by strata bylaws.
Only 55+ age bylaws are legal in BC strata now

Under the Strata Property Act, ss. 123.1 and 123.2, a strata may restrict residents to age 55 or older; any age bylaw set below 55 (19+, 40+, 45+) has been invalid since Nov 24, 2022, when Bill 44 (Building and Strata Statutes Amendment Act, 2022) took effect.
The bylaw restricts who may LIVE in the unit, not who may own it

The Province states people under 55 can own a strata lot in a 55+ corporation but may not be able to reside in it; the exemptions attach to a "specified resident" who meets the age requirement or holds a legacy exemption.
Built-in exemptions (Strata Property Regulation 7.01)

residents who were lawfully living in the unit when a 55+ bylaw passed (legacy residents); live-in caregivers; and — expanded effective May 1, 2023 — a younger spouse or partner, children under 19 in the specified resident's care, and adult children the specified resident cared for before they turned 19.
Rental-restriction bylaws are void province-wide

As of Nov 24, 2022, no strata corporation may have a residential rental-restriction bylaw — all existing ones are invalid, and no bylaw amendment is needed for that to apply. Stratas may still ban or limit SHORT-TERM rentals by bylaw.
Not every 55+ home is a strata

Some 55+ homes are manufactured homes on rented pads, bare-land strata lots, co-op shares, life leases or memberships. Each works differently and each page on this site names which kind a building is.

blocks.text: How to read the MLS 55+ flag

Many 55+ buildings are marked in the MLS with a restricted-age field of 55+. The listing agent types that field, so it can be wrong or left blank, and it says nothing about the exemptions a strata allows or the building's own bylaws. Treat a flagged building as a lead worth checking, not as proof: the proof is the building's bylaws and its Form B.
Where a building has no flag on any recent sale, that is also a clue, not an answer.

items.t: These rules are province-wide strata rules, not a neighbourhood rule, and they apply only where a strata corporation has an age-restriction bylaw.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: the housing stock

items.t: The housing this page is about is strata lots in a strata corporation with a 55+ bylaw, in any building form that corporation takes.
People younger than 55 can own a strata lot in a 55+ corporation but may not be able to live in it, because the bylaw applies to residents, not ownership.
The Province uses the term specified resident for an owner, tenant or occupant who lives in the lot and either meets the age requirement or has a legacy exemption.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: rules that affect buyers

items.t: Only a 55+ age bylaw is allowed now, and any bylaw restricting residents to a younger age such as 19+, 25+ or 40+ is no longer permitted after November 24, 2022.

No strata corporation may have a residential rental-restriction bylaw after November 24, 2022, and all such bylaws are invalid, while a strata may still have or create a bylaw banning or limiting short-term rentals.
A bylaw amendment is made by a 3/4 vote of owners and filed at the Land Title Office, and new or changed bylaws do not take effect until filed, except pet bylaws as the Province notes.

A bylaw cannot contravene the Strata Property Act, the Strata Property Regulation, the Human Rights Code or any other law, and bylaws restricting occupants to age 55+ are expressly permitted within that limit.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: A strata corporation's own bylaws can specify further exemptions beyond the provincially required ones, so two 55+ buildings can lawfully differ.

Strata councils must comply with the BC Human Rights Code when administering the corporation and applying bylaws, and the Province advises councils to seek a knowledgeable strata lawyer for drafting, interpreting and enforcing an age bylaw.
The Land Title Office does not review filed bylaw documents, so a filed bylaw is not automatically an enforceable bylaw.

Before the second annual general meeting, a unanimous vote is required to change bylaws for wholly residential strata corporations, while at the second annual general meeting or later the threshold is a 3/4 vote.
A rule is not a bylaw: rules govern use, safety and condition of common property and cannot govern the use of a strata lot, which only a bylaw can do.
The maximum fine a strata may set is $200 for each contravention of a bylaw other than a short-term rental bylaw, and $50 for each contravention of a rule, as the Province states.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: costs and taxes

items.t: No municipal tax rate exists for this province-wide rules page, and none is stated here.

The provincial item the Province lists is the Speculation and Vacancy Tax (SVT), which applies only in designated taxable areas the Province lists by municipality and regional district, including the City of Surrey, the City of Abbotsford and the District of Mission.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: getting around

items.t: Getting around is not a rule on this page, and no transit fact changes whether a 55+ bylaw is valid, so no route or frequency is claimed here.

blocks.text: BC 55+ Strata Rules: risks and due diligence

items.t: Read the filed bylaws, not the listing, because a bylaw change takes effect only when filed at the Land Title Office and the office does not review what is filed.
Check for a mistaken repeal, because the Province warns strata corporations reviewing bylaws to take care not to mistakenly repeal an age-restriction bylaw when filing a consolidated set.

The Province's own disclaimer states its strata housing information is a basic starting point and is not a substitute for legal advice, which is the correct posture for any exemption that turns on a family's facts.

faq.a: Yes — provincial rules require an exemption for a younger spouse or partner of a resident who meets the age requirement (or holds a legacy exemption). Children can also be exempt in defined cases: a child under 19 in the resident's care, and an adult child the resident cared for before that child turned 19.
faq.q: My spouse is under 55. If we buy in a true 55+ strata nearby, can we both live there?

faq.a: Long-term rental bans no longer exist in BC — every strata rental-restriction bylaw became invalid on Nov 24, 2022. Two catches remain: the tenant still has to satisfy the 55+ age bylaw or an exemption, and a strata can still restrict short-term rentals (and the City regulates short-term rentals under Bylaw 5141).
faq.q: Can I rent out a unit in a 55+ building?

faq.a: Yes, in law: Regulation 7.01 exempts a younger spouse or partner of a qualifying resident, and several complexes state a one-resident rule themselves — Royal Court ("only one owner must be at least 55") and The Wedgewood ("only one resident needs to be over 55").
faq.q: My spouse is under 55. Can we both live in a 55+ strata after we sell?

faq.a: Ownership itself is not age-restricted — the bylaw governs who may reside. The Province states under-55s can own strata lots in a 55+ corporation but may not be able to live in them; a parent who is 55+ can be the resident.
faq.q: I'm under 55. Can I buy in a 55+ complex as an investment or for a parent?

faq.a: Long-term rental bans no longer exist in BC — every strata rental-restriction bylaw became invalid on Nov 24, 2022, including any older "rentals not allowed" record for Manor Ridge. The tenant still has to satisfy the 55+ age bylaw or an exemption, and a strata can still restrict short-term rentals.
faq.q: Can I rent out my unit?

faq.a: Mechanically, yes: the next buyer must also be able to live there under the bylaw — be 55+, be an exempt spouse/partner, caregiver or legacy case, or buy without living in the unit.
faq.q: Does the 55+ restriction shrink my resale buyer pool?

faq.a: Long-term rental bans no longer exist in BC — every strata rental-restriction bylaw became invalid on Nov 24, 2022, whether or not the strata amended its bylaws. A strata can still restrict short-term rentals. The "rentals not allowed" lines in older building sources for this area are stale.
faq.q: Older listings for Shaughnessy strata say "rentals not allowed." Can I rent out a unit I buy there now?

faq.a: Mechanically, yes: the next buyer must also be able to live there under the bylaw — be 55+, be an exempt spouse/partner, caregiver or legacy case, or buy without living in the unit.
faq.q: Does a 55+ restriction shrink my resale buyer pool (at the nearest complexes)?

faq.a: Yes, a younger spouse or partner is exempt when the other resident is a specified resident. The Province lists an exemption for a younger spouse married to, or living in a marriage-like relationship with, a specified resident who meets the age requirement or holds a legacy exemption. That exemption was part of the additional family exemptions that took effect May 1, 2023, alongside the children cases described on the same page.
faq.q: My spouse is under 55 — can we both live in a 55+ strata?

faq.a: What the page does state is that exemptions exist in relationship to a specified resident, that a corporation can specify further exemptions in its own bylaws, and that legacy residents keep their own caregiver and family exemptions. Read the specific corporation's filed bylaws and get legal advice for a survivorship case.
faq.q: What happens to a partner or spouse who survives the 55+ resident?

faq.a: Yes, caregiver exemptions apply to live-in caregivers who provide care to another resident who is dependent on them due to illness, disability or frailty. The Province gives the example of an 87-year-old resident living with a 44-year-old caregiver. The caregiver exemption existed with the November 24, 2022 changes, before the wider family exemptions were added on May 1, 2023.
faq.q: Can a live-in caregiver under 55 live in the unit?

faq.a: No, legacy exemptions protect a resident who was lawfully residing in the lot when the bylaw was passed and who continues to reside there. The Province gives a 36-year-old resident, and two sisters aged 22 and 25, as examples of residents who may continue living in the unit despite a new 55+ bylaw. Legacy residents are also entitled to the caregiver and family exemptions in the future.
